Q: New Tab not responding properly on set interval A:

For purely scientific purposes I decided to bite and play around with this for a bit.

Long story short, the browser prevents this for security reasons, but only in the case where the opened window is from a different origin. This is called the Same-Origin Policy.

You can reproduce this as well by opening the dev console (F12 or Cmd+Opt+I or whatever fancy keyboard shortcut) then typing in:

w = window.open('https://www.google.com')
w.location.href

When I open this from StackOverflow on Chrome, I get this error:

Uncaught SecurityError: Failed to read a named property 'href' from 'Location': An attempt was made to break through the security policy of the user agent.

This is because, per MDN, the WindowsProxy object returned adheres to the same-origin policy (SOP). You can read more about it here, but the idea is that it prevents nasty browser-based attacks by defining a security boundary between origins: site A https://a.com should NOT be able to access stuff from site B https://b.com.

Why does the SOP apply here? Well, suppose this control didn't exist. If I as an attacker made you browse to my evil website, and I was able to open any webpage on your browser, I may be able to see whatever URL address that tab has. This may seem innocuous but it is possible the site may have redirected you or stored sensitive information in the URL (e.g. query or hash parameters).

For the same reason, the SOP also applies when you try reading w.document in the console. If this were possible, then an attacker would be able to read whatever sensitive information was loaded in that browser page (not just the URL address!). This could be, for instance, credit card information.

Now that we know SOP is involved, let's try again, but do it from https://www.google.com.

  1. First, browse to https://www.google.com.
  2. Open the dev console.
  3. Type in w = window.open('https://www.google.com'). The tab should now open. Return to the tab in Step 1.
  4. Type in w.location.href. You should now see that it works without any errors! You can even try setting it like w.location.href = '/search?q=same origin policy' and see the tab change.

Q: AM335x NAND boot – custom bare-metal SPL (no U-Boot) not loaded by BootROM, board resets / beeps A:

@Stas Simonov

SYSBOOT pins are strapped for NAND boot.

SYSBOOT[15:0] configuration:

- Boot mode: NAND

- NAND width: 8-bit

- ECC: BCH8 (512-byte sectors)

- Boot device: GPMC CS0

Hardware:

- AM3352

- NAND connected to GPMC CS0

- CLE/ALE/WE/RE/WAIT0 properly routed

- WAIT0 used for ready/busy

- NAND page size: 2048 bytes

- OOB: 64 bytes

No U-Boot, no Linux.

Pure bare-metal SPL.

No GEL during boot (true cold boot).

Q: How to prevent race condition in AWS DynamoDB and Lambda A:

Use optimistic locking:

In distributed systems like DynamoDB, item version control using optimistic locking prevents conflicting updates. By tracking item versions and using conditional writes, applications can manage concurrent modifications, ensuring data integrity across high-concurrency environments.

Optimistic locking is a strategy used to ensure that data modifications are applied correctly without conflicts. Instead of locking data when it's read (as in pessimistic locking), optimistic locking checks if data has changed before writing it back. In DynamoDB, this is achieved through a form of version control, where each item includes an identifier that increments with every update. When updating an item, the operation will only succeed if that identifier matches the one expected by your application.
